content: 1. The plasma levels of vilazodone can be increased by strong CYP3A4 inhibitors due to their effect on hepatic and intestinal enzyme metabolism. It is recommended to avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. If co-administered, reduce the daily dose of vilazodone to 20 mg and monitor the patient closely. 2. Viloxazine, a weak CYP2D6 inhibitor, may increase the systemic exposure of CYP2D6 substrates by affecting hepatic enzyme metabolism. Use caution, monitor closely, and adjust the dose of the substrate as clinically indicated. 3. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of vinblastine by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter and affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is considered serious; alternative drugs should be used. 4. Lopinavir also increases the levels or effects of vinblastine by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 5. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of vincristine and vincristine liposomal by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter and affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is serious; alternative drugs should be used. 6. Lopinavir increases the levels or effects of vincristine and vincristine liposomal by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 7. Lopinavir increases the levels or effects of vinorelbine by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor closely and modify therapy as needed. 8. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of voclosporin by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. Additionally, ritonavir and voclosporin may increase each other's effects by prolonging the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Lopinavir increases the levels or effects of vorapaxar by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is serious; alternative drugs should be used. 10. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of voriconazole by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, while voriconazole decreases ritonavir levels by increasing its metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 11. Voriconazole increases the levels or effects of lopinavir by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is serious; alternative drugs should be used. 12. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of vortioxetine by affecting CYP2D6 metabolism. Co-administration is serious; alternative drugs should be used. If co-administered with strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, reduce the vortioxetine dose by 50%. 13. Lopinavir increases the levels or effects of voxilaprevir by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is serious; alternative drugs should be used. 14. Ritonavir decreases the levels or effects of warfarin by affecting CYP2C9/10 metabolism. Monitor closely and modify therapy as needed. 15. Zafirlukast increases the levels or effects of ritonavir and lopinavir by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 16. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of zaleplon by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitor closely. 17. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of zanubrutinib by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Reduce the zanubrutinib dose to 80 mg once daily if co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Interrupt dosing as recommended for adverse reactions, and resume the previous dose after discontinuing the CYP3A4 inhibitor. 18. Ritonavir and zidovudine both increase the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Use caution and monitor closely. 19. Lopinavir increases the levels or effects of zileuton by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely, as there is potential for increased toxicity. 20. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of ziprasidone by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitor closely. 21. Lopinavir increases the levels or effects of zolpidem by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitor closely. 22. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of zonisamide by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitor closely. 23. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of zuranolone by affecting CYP2E1 metabolism, while lopinavir decreases its levels. Modify therapy and monitor closely. Reduce the zuranolone dose if co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. 24. Common adverse effects of lopinavir/ritonavir include diarrhea (7-9%), hyperlipidemia (3-39%), nausea (5-16%), rash (12%), abdominal pain (1-11%), ALT elevation (1-11%), headache (2-6%), elevated liver function tests (2-10%), weakness (<9%), hyperuricemia (<5%), flatulence (1-4%), and neutropenia (1-5%). Rare but serious effects include Stevens-Johnson syndrome, erythema multiforme, toxic epidermal necrolysis, nephrolithiasis, and hypersensitivity reactions. 25. Lopinavir/ritonavir is contraindicated with certain drugs, including alpha-1 adrenergic receptor agonists (e.g., alfuzosin), antiarrhythmics (e.g., amiodarone, dronedarone), rifampin, lomitapide, voriconazole, ergot derivatives, and cisapride. 26. Studies in pregnant animals show no treatment-related malformations with lopinavir/ritonavir, but embryonic and fetal toxicities occurred at maternally toxic doses. Newborns exposed in utero and as neonates may have an increased risk of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. 27. The CDC recommends that HIV-1-infected mothers avoid breastfeeding to prevent postnatal transmission of HIV-1, the development of viral resistance, and adverse reactions in the infant. 28. Lopinavir/ritonavir is a protease inhibitor that prevents the cleavage of Gag-Pol polyprotein precursors, leading to the formation of immature, noninfectious viral particles. Lopinavir provides the main antiretroviral effect, while ritonavir inhibits its metabolism to prolong action and increase serum concentration. 29. Lopinavir/ritonavir should not be administered once daily in pediatric patients under 18 years of age; instead, it should be given every 12 hours. Tablets can be taken with or without food, while the oral solution should be taken with food.
